newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pleased with Netanyahu response to Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pleased with Netanyahu response to Jerusalem.

text.p: The United States said on Friday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's opposition to building a Jewish enclave in Arab East Jerusalem was a positive step and appealed for stalled Middle East peace talks to resume.

"I think the important point is that Prime Minister Netanyahu has voiced opposition to the (Jerusalem building) project and said he would work to prevent implementation of the plan," James Foley, deputy spokesman at the State Department, said.
"This is a time for calm and it's a time mostly to return to the negotiating table and we think that the fact that the prime minister says he opposes this is a positive step," Foley added.
Earlier on Friday, Netanyahu's office said the Israeli leader had told the Palestinian Authority he would block construction of the settler enclave "at this time".

The Israeli Jerusalem municipality gave the green light on Thursday night for the project to go ahead. It involves the building of a few dozen houses by American Jewish businessman Irving Moskowitz in the 11,000-strong Arab neighbourhood of Ras al-Amoud.
The municipality's decision was met with anger by Palestinian officials who feared that building Jewish homes in such a sensitive area would lead to a new round of violence.
The status of East Jerusalem, which Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East War, is one of the most volatile issues dividing Israelis and Palestinians.

The PLO wants East Jerusalem as capital of a future Palestinian state and says Israeli moves are aimed at pre-empting talks on the city's fate. Israel says both sides of the city form its "united and eternal" capital.
Foley said it was important to get stalled Israeli-Palestinian peace talks back on track and that the building project was a hindrance to this.
Israeli-Palestinian talks have been deadlocked since Israel started building a Jewish settlement in East jerusalem in March, triggering Palestinian protests.
The United States has been playing a mediating role in the peace process and earlier this week, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said she was hopeful of progress soon in the negotiations.
Diplomatic pressure has mounted in recent weeks for the talks to resume.

U.S. Middle East Coordinator Dennis Ross met Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh this week in Washington in a bid to break the deadlock. Israeli Foreign Minster David Levy and PLO leader Yasser Arafat announced after a meeting in Brussels they had made progress in bridging their differences.
Foley said there were no plans at the moment for Ross to embark on a Middle Eastern peace tour. "He will go when the time is right for another mission," he said.
